title: Why Jack Doohan values childhood neighbour Michael Schumacher
excerpt:
Not many people can say they grew up with a seven-time F1 World Champion as their neighbour, but Haas reserve Jack Doohan can. Not only was Michael Schumacher close friends with Doohan’s father Mick – himself a five-time World Champion on two wheels – but he gifted the young Jack his first go-kart, a moment that helped spark his own journey in motorsport.

In our latest edition of F1 Icons, Doohan explains why Schumacher is his idol in the sport and how that admiration stems from much more than performances and titles…

My father and Michael Schumacher were very close friends. After 1994 they both won their first world championships and somehow were neighbours – one winning on two wheels and one on four wheels. The relationship started there and all my very early years were crossed over with Michael.

I would spend time around the house so, on four wheels, Michael has never been out of the equation for being my idol. I also received my first go-kart from him – for me and my sister – and that was really the start to getting where I am now.

Even if we don’t touch further on what he’s done in the sport, or how successful his F1 story is, I’m incredibly grateful for having such a close relationship with him.

The magnitude of him as an athlete definitely didn’t hit early on. I was a three, five, seven-year-old kid coming home from school and he was just with my father – whatever it might be. When these people are close to you, they’re just another good human like we all are. That’s the basis that gets lost sometimes in the F1 paddock.

At the end of the day, drivers are just normal people. I always say that – apart from being a performer, which essentially we are right? Athlete performers, no different to the circus!

You’re just another Joe Blow. You’ve got the same routine, you wake up, you have your coffee, you do your stuff, you go to work and you come back home.

Hall of Fame: Michael Schumacher

I always wanted to stick so true to those values of being no different to anyone else no matter where on the schedule you are in life. With Michael, I was sort of embedded in that and I really wanted to carry those values in myself.

On track he carried himself with confidence. Obviously, he had good people around him, but he had the right amount of aggressiveness. His calculated tolerance was very assertive and the way he placed the car on track, what he would do with it on track, was extremely strong.

He was always there, you know? Even when things weren’t flowing – whether it be gearbox issues or failures – and he was very, very passionate on and off the track from what I’ve heard from my father.

So, the values are very similar. Especially correlating that between other drivers that my father knew around that time compared to Michael, and hearing the lengths and extent that he worked away from the track, it’s clear to see why he was as successful as he was.

The standouts were being physically fit and being mentally fit. Both him and my dad, instead of getting two hours of work done and saying, ‘I did my deed’ they were consistently going tail for tail and pushing one another. They weren’t just doing what was needed and then moving on.

It's difficult to put his legacy into words, right? And it's going to vary from person to person.

It really comes down to statistics. You can be the most successful Formula 1 driver of all time because in the 1960s, you might have jumped in for one race and won. On a spreadsheet they might have a 100% success rate but are you better than Lewis Hamilton, Michael Schumacher or Sebastian Vettel?

That’s an argument to be said because there will be different perspectives on statistics. Arguing what’s going to be right or wrong really varies from person to person.

For me, regardless of winning seven World Championships over two different decades – with different machinery and different types of vehicles – it’s incredibly inspiring to keep so strong for so long. And then to rejoin in a different time again with a new team fresh off the bat.

There are multiple aspects to praise him, but for me there is so much more beyond his performances inside the car that make Michael Schumacher my F1 idol.

title: The car I loved and the car I loathed – with Nigel Mansell
excerpt:
Nigel Mansell drove a wide range of cars across his F1 career, from Lotus machines he struggled to qualify in to the Williams FW14B with which he ultimately claimed the Drivers’ World Championship title.

But what were the standout designs that he loved and loathed in equal measure? For a new F1.com series, we put those questions to him. Read on to discover his choices, as well as to learn more about each car...

The car Mansell loved: Williams FW11B

“The car I really loved more than anything was the FW11B. It was the fastest car, I think, ever, or [the most] powerful car ever to be developed in F1, with 1,500 horsepower using a Qualifying tyre. That blew your mind.

"Martin Brundle was absolutely spot on: it was a car that wanted to kill you on every corner. So that car… I loved it. I hated it at the same time, because it was trying to kill you! But when you drove that, it was a monster – a monster. You knew when you got out and you were in one piece that you’d done half a decent job.”

F1 technical expert Mark Hughes says…

“The Williams FW11B was the 1987 low-line version of the 1986 FW11. Because the fuel limit had been reduced from 220 litres to 195 in the regulations, the smaller tank allowed the car to be packaged accordingly. There were suspension changes, too, but essentially this was the same concept as before and powered by Honda’s hugely powerful RA167E, which got around the 4-bar turbo boost limit regulated for ’87 to be even more powerful than the unrestricted ’86 engine.”

The car(s) Mansell loathed: Lotus 81B and Lotus 92

“I think the car I really didn’t enjoy at all for a period of time, and loathed, was the first active Lotus car, [the 92], when we were developing that. It was throwing you off the circuit and causing you to have accidents when you were going in a straight line. That was a terrible experience to go through.

“The other car, I think, was the first Lotus that I drove, [the 81B], to try and qualify in a Grand Prix. It was seven inches longer than the normal Lotus car that we were developing, and it wouldn’t turn quickly, because it was too long. It was something that we were trying, but I didn’t enjoy that one either!”

F1 technical expert Mark Hughes says…

“The Lotus 92 was a stop-gap car used by Mansell for the first half of the 1983 season. It initially featured active suspension (the first ever in F1), but this was abandoned after two races because of its unreliability and extra weight. This was Team Lotus’ first season with turbo engines (from Renault) and Lotus had built an entirely different car – the 93T – around that engine. However, Renault could not initially supply enough engines for two cars and so another car had to be built to take the existing non-turbo Cosworth DFV engine. This was the 92 model which Mansell so disliked, especially in active form. The 93T proved uncompetitive and both it and the 92 were replaced by the turbo-powered 94T from the British Grand Prix onwards.

“The Lotus 81B of 1980 was a longer wheelbase version of the original 81. A ground effect car, the 81 struggled in the midfield and it was felt that part of its aerodynamic shortfall was that there was too small a gap between the rear face of the engine and the diffuser, hence a longer wheelbase version was created. This simply created a car with a great reluctance to turn in and was even less competitive than the standard car.”

title: Antonelli interview: The title fight and his Monza mindset
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli is living his best life right now. It's the Italian's second season in Formula 1 and he sits on top of the Drivers' Championship with a 59-point lead over his team mate George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time World Champion whom he replaced at Mercedes in 2025.

Seven F1 Grands Prix have been won by teenagers and Antonelli has won six of them (four-time World Champion Max Verstappen won the other). He took his first pole in China this year and converted that into his first Grand Prix victory. The now 20-year-old went on a run of five wins on the bounce, which included dominating on the streets of Monte Carlo to win the Monaco Grand Prix.

Antonelli has hardly put a foot wrong all year, making the most of a very fast Mercedes and outperforming his more experienced team mate Russell. Even on the weekends when a little error creeps in or he struggles to find the limit, Antonelli has managed to find a way to rescue a strong result – like third in Hungary before the break and second in Zandvoort after.

title: Why Norris has committed to McLaren for the long term
excerpt:
Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, Xavi and Andres Iniesta, Lando Norris and McLaren – there are just some sporting partnerships that are meant to be.

On Saturday, it was announced that the latter will be staying together for the foreseeable future with Norris signing a fresh deal that'll keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.

When Zak Brown got to know a young aspiring racer called Lando Norris, very quickly he formed the opinion that the Briton was World Championship material.

Brown was proved right last year as the 26-year-old fended off team mate Oscar Piastri and a charging Max Verstappen to clinch the Drivers' World Championship crown.

That title success came in year nine of their time together, which began with Norris walking through the doors of the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking in 2017 as a 17-year-old to sign a contract to become test and development driver.

Norris was an instant hit with McLaren and McLaren was an instant hit with Norris. They've grown up together, gone through tough times together and enjoyed success together. They've got each other's respective backs.

That's the kind of environment that Norris thrives in. As he told me in his first interview since the news broke, he's with the people that he wants to be with and "for me, that's calming".

Norris' previous contract ran until at least the end of 2027, so there was no rush to get a new deal done, not least because both Brown and Norris knew they were happy and wanted to continue. So why do another deal already?

Well, following his World Championship victory last year – McLaren's first Drivers' World Championship trophy since Lewis Hamilton triumphed in 2008 – it was always the plan to sit down and discuss extending and improving their arrangement.

Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030

So, in the last few months, they zeroed in on the new terms with both sides sure that, not only did they want to continue beyond 2027, but they wanted to commit for the long-term, which in this case is at least the next four years.

The deal is understood to be a proper commitment from both sides and a clear intention to see it through, rather than a deal that has clauses that could allow one or the other to escape each year.

For Norris, he was keen to do a long-term deal to give him and those around him stability and prevent the persistent rumours about his future floating around and acting as a distraction.

Knowing he'll be at McLaren untll at least the end of 2030, when he'll be 31, also means he can knuckle down and focus on working with his team to add to his win and World Championship tally.

He also believes McLaren have what it takes to win. He believes Brown and Team Principal Andrea Stella are "incredible" leaders and feels the team of people who work with him are the best in the business and are all working in the right direction to bring success. So there really was no reason to change.

For McLaren, they have seen Norris grow from a rising star to a World Champion and were there every step of the way, from signing his first contract and taking his first pole, to sealing his first Grand Prix win and taking the title.

They know what they've got – and they know what he's worth – so understandably, they don't want to let him go.

Signing such an impressive deal that locks him down for at least another four years gives certainty to their shareholders and partners and wards off any admirers – of which there are many – elsewhere in the pit lane.

The driver market could get very spicy in 2028, so locking Norris down early doors sets out their stall and sends a warning signal to rivals.

Trust and belief in each other. Those factors formed the foundations of Norris and McLaren's relationship back in 2017 and, a decade on, they remain the cornerstones.

With team mate Piastri signed up until the end of 2028 – and both sides believed to be very happy with their relationship – McLaren are well set for the future as they battle to create a papaya-coloured dynasty in the years ahead.

title: Norris opens up on why he sees his future at McLaren
excerpt:
Lando Norris is beaming. This isn't uncommon as it's pretty much his baseline, but the Briton's smile and chirpiness is noticeably even brighter when we meet on the uber-cool boulevard of the McLaren Technology Centre for a chat.

This is because Norris is here to talk about a huge new deal that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030. Come the end of that term, he'll have been with the team for 12 years, equaling the record stint countryman Lewis Hamilton had with Mercedes.

It's an extraordinary show of faith in McLaren, with the British team holding the same belief in Norris. And given how perfect Norris and McLaren seem for each other, it's perhaps no surprise that he's chosen to extend his stay with a team where he feels at home.

"I'm very, very excited," he says in his first interview since the news was announced. "McLaren's been my home since the very, very beginning of my career in Formula 1 and I want it to stay that way for as long as possible. We've had a great few years and I'm confident we can achieve that many more times. So I want to stay."

Norris began his F1 journey with McLaren, starting as a test and developing driver, before stepping up as a reserve. He got the nod for a race seat in 2019, racing alongside Carlos Sainz, and went on to take his first podium in Austria 2020 and first pole in Russia 2021.

His first win came in Miami 2024, his first Monaco triumph in 2025 and his first Grand Prix victory on home soil followed that year when he won at Silverstone. He of course would go on to pick up his first World Championship and McLaren's first drivers' title since 2008.

They've seen it all together but they're not done yet. Why change what isn't broken? Especially when you can confirm your long-term future and give yourself some stability.

"I know for a good amount more years that I'm comfortable in terms of I've got a job and I’m where I want to be, and with the people that I want to be with, and for me that's calming," he says. "I can focus on a job I need to do and as a team we can also focus on the job that we want to do."

He adds: "You can always see results as most important and 99% of the time I think they are, but I would say there's leeway, there's leverage in terms of just the fact I'm with the people that I want to be with, people that I enjoy spending my career with.

Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030

"I don't want to be bouncing around teams and doing different things. I want be where I'm happy and, even when we weren't winning, I was also happy to be part of McLaren.

"I think something I always know for my future is I want results of course – the team know that just as much as anyone – but I also just want to be wherever I'm most happy and even if we're not winning like the beginning of this year, it's not like I want to change team.

"I'm still very happy with who I am with and happy to kind of fight through whatever we have coming up."

'I don’t want to distract my team'

Fighting back McLaren are. After a slow start, which included McLaren failing to take the start in the opener in Australia and both failing to start at the following race in China, the reigning World Champions are fighting back.

An upgrade in Hungary before the break hauled them into contention and opened the door for Norris to secure his and the team's first victory of the season. That package was completed with more parts after the break in Zandvoort, with Norris taking pole and a second successive victory.

He's still someway off in the championship fight, as he sits 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli, but he and McLaren have the momentum – and if last year is anything to go by (when Max Verstappen sliced through a 104-point deficit to force a title decider in Abu Dhabi) Norris is very much in with a chance of defending his title.

That response is just what Norris knows McLaren are capable of, but that form didn't trigger this renewal. Those chats had been in the diary since he won the world title in Abu Dhabi last year.

Norris knew he wanted to stay and McLaren knew they wanted to keep them. To warn off admirers from elsewhere on the grid and to stamp out any ambiguity about his future, they were both keen to extend.

Drivers' Championship after Zandvoort

"It's a continuation of my last [contract]," he says. "We just want to be able to focus on doing our best job, to extract performance, to get the most out of everyone and focus on the importance that we do not get caught up in the mess of everyone else deciding contracts.

"I don’t want to distract my team, I don't want to distract the guys and girls here that are here to give me the best car possible and for me to do the best job for them.

"We want to focus on our jobs and not think about all the noise that goes on in the sidelines. So for me it's 'guys I'm here to stay. I want to be with you for a long time' and it gives them a good boost, gives me a good boost and together it means we can just focus."

'I want to make this my home'

Norris also believes in the set-up McLaren have, led by CEO Zak Brown and Team Principal Andrea Stella. "Zak is a very good leader, he's a very good boss," says Norris.

"As much as we get on and we just, we love racing, we want to win together, we enjoy golf and things, he is still my boss so he still gives me a kick whenever I do something wrong or if I'm not doing something well enough.

"That's always what I want – someone that's honest and who gives me the brutal truth no matter what it is and that something that's very important to me.

"At the same time I have that very much so with Andrea, and Andrea is for me – and of course I'm biased and this is the only place I've been – but we have had a few different team principals and he is most certainly the most influential over the team.

"He is an incredible leader, someone who knows how to bring a group of people together and also knows how to lead individuals such as me in terms of how I can go out and increase my performance every day and be a better person.

"So, even if I could change anything with where I am now, I wouldn't and I think that's the perfect reason."

Will Norris, who will be 31 when this next deal expires, ever leave McLaren? There's a very good chance he won't.

"I want to make this my home," says the Briton, who holds the record for the most starts for McLaren. "I want it to be the place that I am at for a very, very long time and maybe even forever.

"There are more nice things that just allow me to work better here and live better here, and that's an amazing thing."

title: Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030
excerpt:
Lando Norris has committed his future to McLaren after signing a new deal that will extend his stay at the British team until at least the end of 2030, with a multi-year option to commit beyond that date.

The Briton joined McLaren in 2017 as a test and development driver before earning promotion to the grid as a race driver for 2019.

The 26-year-old has since gone on to claim 13 Grand Prix victories, 18 pole positions and 48 podiums – as well as his maiden World Championship in 2025. Additionally he has now raced in 163 Grands Prix for the team, more than any other McLaren driver in history.

His previous deal is believed to have been set to expire at the end of 2027, but McLaren moved to lock him down for the foreseeable future with a fresh contract extension.

As well as confirming his future, Norris will also be gifted an MCL39 by the squad, which he raced during his title-winning season last year.

“McLaren is my home, and I’m very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," Norris said.

"When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships. We’ve achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we’re capable of achieving it.

"I can’t wait to get back in the car in Monza and I’m very excited about what the future holds for us, both over the rest of this season, and in the coming years.”

McLaren CEO, Zak Brown, said: “I’m incredibly pleased to be signing a new contract with Lando, extending his commitment with McLaren until at least 2030. His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves.

"Together with Andrea [Stella], Oscar [Piastri] and the wider team, Lando has helped drive McLaren into a new papaya era of success, helping us go from the back of the grid, to double consecutive constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and our first Drivers’ Championship in 17 years. We are extremely excited about what lies ahead and remain fully focused on continuing to compete for wins and championships.”

McLaren Team Principal, Andrea Stella, added: "Lando has been an integral part of McLaren’s journey and success over the last nine years, and we are delighted to continue our partnership with him through to at least 2030.

"He is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team.

“Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together.

"With him and Oscar, we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1.”

By the end of the current agreement, Norris will be 31 and have spent 12 years with McLaren, matching the stint Lewis Hamilton achieved with Mercedes.

His deal expires at the same time as his rival and friend Max Verstappen, who recently committed to Red Bull, whom he joined in 2016, until the end of 2030.

Norris' team mate Oscar Piastri, meanwhile, is contracted with McLaren up until the end of 2028, having signed a fresh deal ahead of the 2025 campaign. That gives McLaren stability for at least the next two Formula 1 campaigns.

title: Why Aston Martin is bringing house music to F1 fans
excerpt:
Earlier this week, Aston Martin announced a partnership with British record label and house music specialists Defected. The pairing of motorsport and music is nothing new, but with a huge growth of fans in both F1 and house, the collaboration feels like it’s coming at just the right time.

House music as a genre was born in Chicago at the start of the ‘80s and has only grown in popularity, becoming mainstream with tracks frequently populating the global charts.

It’s already got a presence in Formula 1; just take a look at a driver’s social media round-up and you’ll likely see it paired to a house tune – yes, Oscar Piastri, we’re looking at you.

Aston Martin have taken this to another level with their partnership with Defected Records, hosting a ‘Driven By Sound’ pop-up in Central London for their I/AM members. From the outside, this pairing might feel like an interesting choice, but it’s a collaboration that makes a lot of sense.

“We want to associate ourselves with iconic properties and Defected absolutely ticks that box,” Rob Bloom, Aston Martin's Chief Marketing Officer explained.

“Defected is the belief that house music exists on and off the dance floor, and that community culture is so much more than just the music. We are absolutely in that mindset as the Aston Martin Formula 1 Team, and we want to engage fans and welcome them into our world, whether you go to a Grand Prix or not.

“The Aston Martin brand is 100 years old, but it's always been a cultural phenomenon. It existed way beyond its core product, we are very comfortable – in culture – punching outside of category, and that's the space we play, in which we are so much more than just a car company or motorsports team.”

How Alonso used a unique strategy to earn P9 in Zandvoort

Music has always had links with Formula 1, from its association with ‘The Chain’ by Fleetwood Mac to the incredible album created for F1 The Movie – the two passions always find a way of coming together. However, with so many genres to pick from, why did Aston Martin gravitate towards house?

“There's a natural alignment," Bloom continues. "If you look at house music and F1, we both bring scale and intimacy. Two global properties, in house music and Formula 1, and there are 825 million F1 fans out there in the world: it's truly global.

"But, when you bring fans together at little moments like this, that's where you get the intimacy. You can have huge global platforms that still have very intimate personal relationships and experiences as part of it.”

For Aston Martin's I/AM members, the Soho pop-up is a great chance to get up close and personal to the team, with activations that include a complimentary coffee whilst enjoying DJ sets from Sam Divine and RUZE, or a run club that’s hosted on the Sunday.

Once inside the venue, there’s also plenty to see: from Fernando Alonso’s race suit and helmet to a sound wall which invites guests to listen to a mix of team radio, the Honda power unit and team radio from their F1 ACADEMY driver Mari Boya.

“Dance music has evolved a lot since I've been doing this,” said Simon Marlin, a house producer from The Shapeshifters. “There's nothing more unique than finding friends on the dance floor.

"Defected Croatia is a great example of people that had never met each other 10 years ago, and now are the best of friends, crying with each other because the festival finished this year.

"That can only happen through shared experiences that are delivered in a way that makes you feel special, that makes you go beyond what you expected. They're the moments that bring people together, and house music is the biggest and best platform to do that. It's such a feel-good factor.”

The exploration of house music in Formula 1 has been seen through the genre’s biggest DJs collaborating on F1 Tracks – the official F1 playlist – or huge names like Diplo performing at this year’s Singapore Grand Prix. The crossover between passions is clear, and who knows? Perhaps another driver will take up DJing after retirement – much like Alonso's compatriot Jaime Alguersuari, who now goes by the stage name Squire.

title: 10 unexpected careers F1 drivers pursued away from the track
excerpt:
For Formula 1 drivers, retirement does not necessarily mean leaving the sport behind. Plenty swap the cockpit for the commentary box, while others become team bosses, ambassadors or driver managers – keeping one foot firmly planted in the paddock.

But for some, life away from F1 has taken a rather different turn. Across the decades, former drivers have traded racing cars for everything from fishing trawlers and farms to DJ decks and even political office.

Here are 10 F1 drivers whose careers away from the track took them somewhere rather unexpected...

Niki Lauda – Airline entrepreneur

There aren't many things Niki Lauda didn't accomplish in Formula 1. The Austrian won three World Championships across two spells in the sport, famously battled James Hunt for the 1976 World Championship and eventually returned to the paddock in senior roles with Ferrari, Jaguar and Mercedes.

But even while his driving career was still unfolding, Lauda had another fascination entirely – aviation. He established Lauda Air in 1979, the same year he first stepped away from F1, and began building what would eventually become an international airline operating long-haul services around the world. After returning to Formula 1 with McLaren in 1982 and claiming a third World Championship, he retired for good three years later and turned his attention to aviation full-time, later expanding his involvement with ventures such as Niki and Laudamotion.

Being a three-time World Champion and playing a major role in Mercedes' future dominance would probably constitute enough careers for most people. But Lauda somehow found time to become a successful airline entrepreneur as well.

Paolo Barilla – Pasta executive

Paolo Barilla's time in Formula 1 was relatively brief. The Italian made his debut for Minardi at the 1989 Japanese Grand Prix and went on to enter 15 Grands Prix across two seasons, starting nine of them and recording a best finish of 11th. His racing CV extended well beyond F1, however – most notably including an outright victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1985.

By 1991, Barilla was ready for something different. Fortunately, there was a rather famous family business waiting for him.

He joined Barilla France before being appointed Deputy Chairman of the Barilla Group in 1994, a position he continues to hold. More than three decades after leaving the F1 grid, his two careers even collided when Barilla became an official Formula 1 partner in 2025.

Speaking at the announcement, Barilla said: “A lightning-fast F1 car and a delicious plate of pasta: what do they have in common? At first, it may not be obvious, but behind both, and the effort that goes into making them, are skilled professionals, passionate and determined, driven by the desire to keep improving.”

Perhaps racing cars and pasta have more in common than first meets the eye...

Carlos Reutemann – Politician

Carlos Reutemann came agonisingly close to becoming an F1 World Champion, losing the 1981 title to Nelson Piquet by a single point after arriving at the season finale in Las Vegas at the top of the standings.

By the time he stepped away from F1 in 1982, the Argentine had accumulated 12 Grand Prix victories and established himself as one of his country's greatest drivers behind five-time champion Juan Manuel Fangio. After briefly returning to rallying, Reutemann then entered an arena that could arguably be every bit as competitive as Formula 1 – politics.

In 1991, he was elected governor of his home province of Santa Fe, serving until 1995 before returning for a second term between 1999 and 2003. He then moved into Argentina's National Senate, winning re-election in both 2009 and 2015 and remaining a senator until his death in 2021.

Reutemann's political profile grew so significantly that he was considered a serious potential candidate for the Argentine presidency – but declined to run in 2002. From fighting for the F1 title to potentially fighting for the country's highest office, his competitive career certainly didn't end at the chequered flag.

Alex Ribeiro – Sports chaplain

Anyone familiar with Alex Ribeiro's racing cars might not be too surprised by the direction his life eventually took.

The Brazilian competed in F1 during the 1970s for Hesketh, March and Copersucar-Fittipaldi, but became just as recognisable for the enormous 'Jesus Saves' message carried on his F2 racing machinery. His Christian faith was an important part of his identity throughout his career and became an even bigger part of his life after leaving F1.

Ribeiro became heavily involved with the organisation Atletas de Cristo – Athletes of Christ – supporting sportspeople across Brazil and serving as its executive director. His work took him far beyond motorsport, with Ribeiro acting as a chaplain to Christian members of the Brazilian national football team across several World Cups, including the victorious 1994 campaign in the United States.

Remarkably, his second career even brought him back into the F1 paddock. Ribeiro later drove the sport's Medical Car while also carrying out chaplaincy work – meaning that even decades after his Grand Prix career ended, he found a very different way to continue helping athletes at the highest level.

Jaime Alguersuari – DJ and producer

When Jaime Alguersuari made his F1 debut for Toro Rosso at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix, the 19-year-old became the youngest driver the sport had ever seen at that point.

But just a few years later, his life looked completely different. After losing his Toro Rosso seat at the end of 2011, Alguersuari continued competing in categories including Formula E and GT racing. However, his passion for motorsport gradually disappeared and, still only in his mid-20s, the Spaniard decided to walk away from racing entirely.

Fortunately, another passion had been developing alongside it. Alguersuari had been producing electronic music even during his F1 career and eventually turned his attention to it full-time under the name Squire, a nod to his second surname, Escudero. He has since released music and performed internationally as a DJ and producer.

Plenty of drivers have talked about needing to find a new rhythm after leaving Formula 1. Alguersuari took that rather more literally.

Jody Scheckter – Farmer

Jody Scheckter's F1 career ended with one of the ultimate achievements already secured. The South African won the 1979 World Championship with Ferrari before retiring from the sport after one final season with the Scuderia in 1980.

His first move away from racing was already somewhat unconventional. Scheckter built a successful firearms training technology business in the United States – but even that would eventually give way to another dramatic change of direction…farming.

Scheckter established Laverstoke Park Farm in Hampshire, developing thousands of acres around natural and biodynamic farming principles. The operation became home to sheep, cattle and a particularly sizeable population of water buffalo, whose milk was used to make mozzarella. The farm also produced everything from meat and ice cream to sparkling wine.

Jacques Villeneuve – Singer-songwriter

Jacques Villeneuve achieved more than most racing drivers could dream of before turning 27. He won the Indianapolis 500 and CART title in 1995, arrived in Formula 1 the following year and became World Champion with Williams in just his second season.

But Villeneuve had another creative interest bubbling away in the background. He had been writing lyrics and playing guitar for years, and after his final F1 appearance in 2006 he was finally able to give music rather more attention.

The result was Private Paradise, a 13-track acoustic album released in 2007 featuring songs in both French and English. Villeneuve wrote six of the tracks himself, including Father, which paid tribute to his late father and Ferrari legend Gilles Villeneuve.

It would be fair to say that Villeneuve's musical career never quite reached the heights of his racing one – Private Paradise did not exactly trouble the upper reaches of the charts. But how many F1 World Champions can say they followed up a title-winning racing career by releasing a bilingual acoustic-rock album?

Alex Zanardi – Paralympic champion

Alex Zanardi's journey after Formula 1 is unlike any other on this list.

The Italian raced in F1 across the 1990s, but enjoyed his greatest success in America, becoming a two-time CART champion in 1997 and 1998. In 2001, during a CART race at the Lausitzring in Germany, Zanardi suffered a devastating accident which resulted in the loss of both of his legs.

Remarkably, his racing career did not end there. Zanardi returned to competitive motorsport with adapted controls before discovering handcycling – initially taking part in marathons before setting his sights on the Paralympic Games.

At London 2012 he won two individual gold medals at Brands Hatch, a circuit where he had raced more than two decades earlier, along with silver in the team relay. Four years later in Rio, he added another two golds and a silver to take his career Paralympic tally to six medals.

Zanardi, who passed away in May 2026 at the age of 59, became one of the most decorated Para cyclists of his generation.

Stefan Johansson – Artist

Stefan Johansson's racing career took him almost everywhere. The Swede drove for Ferrari and McLaren in Formula 1, competed in IndyCar and eventually won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1997.

But alongside all that racing, Johansson had quietly begun developing a very different skill.

He started painting in 1986 after the death of his close friend and fellow F1 driver Elio de Angelis and has since explained that painting helped him process the experience.

After stepping back from driving, Johansson channelled more of his energy into art and design. His work has often drawn directly from racing – including abstract pieces designed to capture the sensation of speed, paintings of moments from his own career and even an art car based around a Porsche fitted with an F1-derived TAG turbo engine.

Innes Ireland – Commercial fisherman

Innes Ireland was never likely to choose a particularly conventional retirement.

As a former paratrooper and engineer before reaching Formula 1, Ireland became one of the sport's great characters during the late 1950s and 1960s. He also earned a significant place in Lotus history when he won the 1961 United States Grand Prix at Watkins Glen International – the team's first World Championship Grand Prix victory.

After his racing career wound down, Ireland returned to Scotland and swapped racing cars for fishing boats. Based around Kirkcudbright, he operated trawlers and went out to sea himself, with local records showing that he bought and refitted an ageing Norwegian trawler called Vetrung as well as another Norwegian vessel which he converted for lobster fishing.

But despite the dramatic change of machinery, some old habits apparently remained. When a well-known motorsport magazine visited Ireland in the 1970s, he arrived back from a fishing expedition and proceeded to spin his boat twice in the narrow harbour as the journalists watched from shore.

Different vehicle, same Innes Ireland.

Honorary mention: Nigel Mansell – Member of the Magic Circle

Nigel Mansell might not have turned magic into a second career, but the 1992 World Champion did take the hobby seriously enough to become a member of The Magic Circle – one of the world’s most prestigious societies for magicians.

Mansell took up magic later in life and has spoken about how learning tricks helped challenge and retrain his brain, eventually earning his place in the famous society after demonstrating his skills.

Not quite a career change – but becoming a bona fide member of The Magic Circle is a pretty impressive retirement hobby.
